title: Tech Note: The 128th Byte
author: Olivier Deschanels
featured_technology: Record header, microstructure, and data layout
Automatic structure/microstructure comparison on record load
APPLY TO SELECTION for forcing immediate record conversion

historical_commentary.text: Olivier Deschanels (4D, S.A.) explains why 4D moved to a single data file (unlike multi-file architectures used by many competing databases of the era) and how that file is broken into fixed 128-byte blocks, with each record carrying a 22-byte header plus a per-record 'microstructure' (field types and offsets) that lets 4D defer applying structure changes until a record is actually loaded and re-saved, and why fields therefore cannot be deleted (only their type changed) in the classic engine. This describes 4D's original classic storage engine, which was later replaced by the 4D SQL/CoreData engine (from 4D v11 SQL onward); while the general single-file design philosophy persisted, the exact 128-byte-block/microstructure mechanics described are no longer how current 4D databases store data, making this a historical rather than practical technical reference today.
related_updates: 4D replaced its classic 128-byte-block data engine with the 4D SQL/CoreData storage engine starting around 4D v11 SQL (2007)

Field deletion restrictions and manual structure-conversion techniques described here (e.g., forcing conversion via APPLY TO SELECTION) reflect the classic engine and do not describe current 4D storage internals
The single-file .4DD/.data deployment/backup simplicity philosophy described has been preserved conceptually in later 4D storage engines
